KEY MESSAGE 1...
There remains a severe thunderstorm risk this afternoon- 
evening, and even with a potential wave of convection Wednesday
morning. However, the bigger timeframe of concern has shifted 
to primarily late Wednesday afternoon into evening.

A wave of non-severe thunderstorms passed through the region 
this morning with locally heavy rainfall, extending from the
greater Ithaca and Binghamton NY areas into Susquehanna-Wayne
Counties PA. Despite the shallow warm frontal regime that has
set up straddling our region, we are between waves aloft and  
have a lack of a trigger. We will continue to monitor for
a diurnal-heating forced convective cells that could still
manage to pop up in Northeast PA but overall the severe
thunderstorm risk has somewhat scaled back as shear values have
decreased. Whatever we do still get from heating will wane
quickly this evening for a fairly quiet night with patchy fog.

The frontal zone will become even more pronounced Wednesday.
Upper flow will steadily increase through the day, with a couple
waves passing through to interact with the temperature gradient
zone. Precipitable water values, after stepping back a bit 
overnight, will ramp back up a bit with a lead shortwave in the 
morning and then top off approaching 2 inches with a stronger 
wave by Wednesday evening. Undercutting these waves aloft, will 
be the light southeast flow encroaching at the surface, 
advancing around high pressure over New England to push in some 
marine layer. So there will indeed be a gradient of conditions 
for the area, with highs ranging form only upper 60s-lower 70s 
Poconos-Catskills to lower-mid 80s in Finger Lakes. 

With the lead shortwave, there is considerable uncertainty for
whether it will generate and sustain a line of convection/for 
how long. Some convection allowing models (CAMS) allow it to 
bring a decaying line of convection into the region during the 
morning. It will be driven by aloft-processes instead of being 
surface-based, so the severe risk may be limited. However, on 
the mesoscale we will have to see if it generates renewed 
convection with boundaries on the way out, which could lead to
isolated strong to severe.

Wednesday afternoon, convective available potential energy
(CAPE) climbs in a warm and very humid environment. As with
today, there may be a lack of triggers between waves. However,
this time a stronger wave in projected to enter the area late
afternoon through evening which will harness whatever CAPE
builds up before then. Convective parameters especially more
comfortably on the warm side of the frontal zone appear quite
concerning late Wednesday. Surface-rooted storms that fire with
the wave will then ride up the shallow warm front, with time 
becoming more elevated. However, shallow warm fronts can be 
quite problematic with the shear that the generate in the low 
levels. There will be an overlapping zone of elevated helicity,
which is why isolated tornadoes cannot be ruled out in addition
the downburst potential from storm cores. Mitigating factors are
limited midlevel temperature lapse rates as thermal profiles
approach moist-adiabatic, and the trend towards a later arrival
of the wave which is less able to harness diurnal heating.

Though the parade-route of passing shortwaves gradually presses
south into Thursday, it is still close enough to pose a threat
for stronger thunderstorms at least in Northeast PA, and
elevated showers-embedded thunder farther north across the rest
of the region.

KEY MESSAGE 2... 

With a stalled front and high precipitable water values 
Wednesday into Thursday morning of around 2 inches, potential
for locally heavy rain and at least isolated flash flooding is 
a concern. Though there will be a gradient of severe weather
parameters that lessens east of I-81, the parameters for
excessive rainfall will exist well north and east of the frontal
zone in addition to along it. Warm cloud depths will be quite
high, above 12kft agl, and a very moist low level jet will keep
feeding in moisture. The High-Resolution Ensemble Forecast
(HREF) model suite probability matched mean continues to depict
stripes of 2-3 inches. Even though exact locations could 
change, there in increasing confidence in the scenario leading 
to excessive rainfall amounts somewhere within our general 
area. Conjunction of parameters puts more of the focus on 
Central NY to Northern Tier of PA versus points farther south. 
Timing of waves, and frontal zone location at those times, will 
be key for who ends up with flash flooding, with potential for 
isolated amounts above 3 inches. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...

After the busier pattern through Thursday, the extended Labor
Day Weekend actually looks pretty benign. Friday into early 
next week, the large ridge in the central US retrogrades west 
with the trough in the northeast nudging into the mid Atlantic. 
This will help the flow become more northerly with seasonably
